Triggers.value: Specific body parts associated with the event

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
Being alone in a room or building
hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings

Threat.value: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

vignette:
Erik is a twenty-one-year-old married man who has been unemployed since the night his wife, Mia, was attacked during a robbery outside their apartment building six months ago. He arrived seconds after it happened and found her on the pavement, a deep gash across her forearm, blood pooling in the gutter. That image-her arm, the wound-stayed with him like a photograph he could not turn away from, fixed and silent. He can still smell the metallic scent of the blood, though when he tries to describe what he saw, the words collapse; it does not feel like something language can hold. 

In the weeks that followed, Erik began avoiding the television entirely-any programme that showed a fight, a knife, even a sudden injury could drop him back into that alleyway. He also found himself unable to stay alone in the apartment while Mia worked her shifts. The silence made the flashbacks worse: moments when he would suddenly feel his heart pound, his skin dampen, as if the attack were happening again right there in the living room. Night after night, sleep barely came; he lay rigid, listening for footsteps, for voices, for anything that might signal danger. 

His body never seemed to understand that the event was over. Every time a stranger made a fast movement-a hand reaching for a wallet, a person spinning around on the street-Erik's muscles locked, his breath shortened. He had come to believe his own reactions had turned against him, that his body was acting like an enemy he could not control. The feeling that he was no longer capable of protecting the people he loved, that he could not even rely on himself to stay calm, only sharpened his attention to the world around him. Because he now believed he could not trust his own instincts, things he would once have dismissed-a door slamming in the hallway, a stranger's quick glance in his direction-began to feel like urgent signals that something terrible was about to happen. A casual comment from his mother-in-law about how the family was doing would immediately trigger the visual memory of Mia's wound, and then he would be scanning the room for any person who looked suspicious, anyone who might be planning harm. 

Because he dreaded being alone, Erik started spending long afternoons in a nearby coffee shop, hoping the crowd would distract him from the flashbacks. But the crowd itself became a source of threat: he watched people's hands, their sudden turns, interpreting each as potential danger. The more he watched, the more suspicious actions he saw, and the cycle tightened. When the overwhelm became unbearable, he would hurt himself physically-pressing his fingernails into his arm or using a small blade-because the sharp pain was the only thing that momentarily cut through the racing thoughts and the feeling that he was losing his mind. That act of self-harm, however, only reinforced his conviction that he could not trust his own body, and it deepened his vigilance, making him even more alert to the next perceived threat. 

Avoiding media did not prevent the memories; instead, the photographic images grew more vivid, and the smells seemed to return at random moments, as if his brain had stored them without his permission. Each time he tried not to think about the event, the nonverbal, fragmented quality of the memory convinced him he would never be able to make sense of what happened, and that belief made him feel even less capable of handling everyday life. He stopped applying for jobs because he was certain he would break down if anyone made a sudden comment about family or if a colleague's arm brushed against him. 

It was Mia who finally persuaded him to seek help, after she found him one night sitting on the bathroom floor, having cut his forearm-the same spot as her scar-and crying because he could not remember why he had done it. What frightens Erik most now is the possibility that he will never regain the sense of being able to rely on himself, that his body and his mind have permanently turned into something foreign. He hopes, more quietly, that someone can show him how to stop the images from coming back, even if he cannot yet put what happened into words.

violations.explanation: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals directly cause triggers; negative appraisals sharpen attention (a maladaptive strategy) but do not directly lead to triggers.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals directly cause triggers; negative appraisals sharpen attention (a maladaptive strategy) but do not directly lead to triggers.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
